Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• Left-sided, intermittent conductive-sounding hearing loss × 6 weeks.  
• Intermittent unilateral tinnitus (improves with background noise).  
• Mild disequilibrium; no true vertigo, pain, discharge, fever, chest pain, or palpitations.  
• No cotton-bud use; no prior ear pathology except brief episode 1 year ago.

Working diagnosis  
• Cerumen impaction causing conductive hearing loss and tinnitus—most likely given presentation and ease of exclusion.

Considerations  
• Ménière’s disease (medium likelihood)—fluctuating loss + tinnitus + mild balance symptoms.  
• Serous otitis media / Eustachian-tube dysfunction (medium).  
• Acoustic neuroma (low-medium)—important to rule out if symptoms persist after initial management.

Plan  
1. Arrange face-to-face clinic visit within 4–5 days for otoscopy to assess for wax, effusion, or other external/middle-ear causes.  
2. Provide patient with tinnitus education leaflet (link placed in notes).  
3. Advise patient to re-book video review earlier if symptoms worsen.  
4. Further management guided by otoscopy:  
   • If cerumen impaction—ear toileting or cerumenolytic drops.  
   • If normal exam—consider audiogram and ENT referral to evaluate for sensorineural loss, Ménière’s disease, or acoustic neuroma.

- Optometry referral for visual concerns or regular screening:  Not recorded.  
- Audiometry referral if hearing issues suspected:  To be considered after otoscopic evaluation.  
- Social work or housing support referral if social determinants affect health:  Not recorded.  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Cerumen impaction – High likelihood: gradual unilateral conductive loss with tinnitus; first-line exclusion planned.  
2. Ménière’s disease – Medium likelihood: unilateral fluctuating loss + tinnitus + disequilibrium, though vertigo mild.  
3. Serous otitis media/Eustachian-tube dysfunction – Medium likelihood: effusion may cause muffled hearing and tinnitus without pain or fever.
